fields.title: Polka: Team Tripled in Size, but Releases Got Slower
fields.summary: The team grew from four to eleven, and everything slowed down. Decide what to fix.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do this quarter?
fields.brief/role: You are the PM for Polka.
fields.brief/company: Polka is a fictional inventory app for small stores. 100 client stores.
fields.brief/context: Six months ago, the team had four people and released every two weeks. Now there are eleven, and it takes 22 days from decision to user. The CTO is asking to hire two more developers.
fields.brief/objective: Understand why things got slower and decide what to change.
fields.brief/constraints: There is a budget for hiring, but only for two people. One quarter.
fields.brief/task: Choose what you will do and justify your decision.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: More hands do not mean faster delivery
fields.learnTakeaway/body: When active work takes up only a fifth of the cycle time, speeding it up is pointless, and adding people is harmful: new tasks just join the same queues and make them longer. The first thing to do is measure where work is stuck and reduce the number of concurrent tasks. Also, a quick check for retrospectives: if a problem is brought up for the third time, the team likely lacks the authority to solve it.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Retrospectives are held every two weeks, everyone attends.

The last four times, the same issues were raised: "urgent tasks disrupt plans" and "design takes forever."

There are no records of accepted changes; they just discuss and disperse at the end.

Urgent tasks come directly from sales to developers, bypassing the queue: there were 27 such tasks this quarter.

The team has brought up the designer for the fourth consecutive time; the decision on their workload is made by the Product Director, not the team.

The definition of "done" varies: two people think it's after code review, the rest think it's after testing.

The five new hires started at different times; none of them had an onboarding talk about working rules.
fields.evidenceCards/2/title: What is happening with the people
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
11 people: 6 developers, a QA engineer, an analyst, a designer (half-time), you, and a team lead.

There is only one QA engineer. The testing queue is the most noticeable in the measurement after design.

Code review is done by two senior developers; both are overloaded with their own tasks.

Two new developers completed only one task each in two months: the rest of the time was spent waiting for reviews and clarifications.

The team lead believes hiring is necessary: "people are overloaded."

Yet, when asked what they are busy with, six reply that they are running three to four tasks simultaneously.

During the quarter, two people said in 1-on-1 meetings that "it's unclear who decides what."
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Clients complain that fixes take too long: the average time from complaint to fix is a month.

Sales promised three stores faster scanner performance this quarter.

The Product Director suggests splitting the team into two by product areas.

Hiring a developer takes 6–8 weeks plus a month to onboard.

There is a budget for two people until the end of the year.

No cycle time measurements had been done before: the 22 days were calculated by you last week.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Fix the wait time, not the work speed
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Rely on the measurement: reduce the number of concurrent tasks, remove the release window, offload design and review, and ensure the retrospective leads to a single action item with an owner.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The measurement is already done and it settles the argument: active work takes 4 days out of 22, the rest is waiting. Hiring two more people would have just added tasks to the same queues.
You limit the number of concurrent tasks to six instead of nineteen. In two weeks, the cycle time drops to 14 days — solely because of this.
You eliminate the release window: releases are automated and take 20 minutes, yet you were waiting three days out of a year-old habit.
You distribute code reviews among four people instead of two, and involve the designer at the requirements stage.
You escalate the designer's workload issue to the Product Director — the team had discussed it for four retrospectives in a row without the authority to solve it.
You restructure the retrospective: one change, an owner, a deadline, and reviewing the previous action item at the start. You route urgent sales tasks through yourself: in the next quarter, there are 6 instead of 27.
By the end of the quarter, the cycle time is 9 days with eleven people.
Trade-off: the team lead felt you refused to solve the overload problem, and resolving this took several meetings.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The team lead is right: people are overloaded, there are more tasks than hands. The budget is there, start hiring now.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Hiring takes seven weeks, plus another month to onboard — meaning the effect only starts next quarter.
By that point, concurrent tasks reach 24, and the queue for code review and testing grows longer: there are still only two reviewers and one QA engineer.
Cycle time increases from 22 to 26 days.
The two new hires, like the previous two, complete only one task each in their first two months.
Client complaints about fix times intensify.
Trade-off: hands were added to a step that takes 4 days out of 22, while the bottlenecks remained untouched and grew longer.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: The Product Director suggests splitting by area. Fewer people in the flow means fewer queues.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Splitting indeed reduces coordination within each part, and this helps: the cycle time drops to 18 days.
But shared resources remain shared: one designer for two teams, one QA engineer, and the same two reviewers. Now, the queues also compete between the teams.
Urgent tasks from sales continue to come directly to both.
A quarter later, both teams bring up the exact same issues at retrospectives as before.
Trade-off: the structure was changed instead of the bottlenecks; some of the effect was accidental, while the root cause of the slowdown was left untouched.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Five new hires, no one has discussed the rules, "done" is understood differently, and two don't know who decides what. Gather the team and agree.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
A two-hour conversation resolves real issues: a unified definition of "done" is established, it becomes clear who makes decisions in case of disagreement, and new hires stop waiting two days for clarifications.
The cycle time is reduced from 22 to 19 days — there is an effect, but it is small.
The bulk of the wait time remains: nineteen tasks in progress, a release window, one QA engineer, one designer.
At the next retrospective, "design takes forever" is heard again, and this is still outside the team's authority.
Trade-off: necessary work was done to fix misunderstandings, but it didn't address the math of the queues.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: No measurement of where work is stuck: waiting is not separated from active work
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Process discussions do not end with an action item that has an owner and a deadline
